Chapter 6: Interrupting Overthinking in the Moment—Practical Tools for Everyday Calm.
So, once you’ve started building those supportive environments and healthy habits, what comes next? Well, it’s all about catching overthinking right as it pops up—and having a few go-to tools to break the cycle. Because, let’s face it, even with the best intentions, those old mental patterns can sneak back in—especially when you’re stressed or things feel uncertain.
The trick is to notice those moments early. Maybe it’s a comment from a coworker, an unexpected change of plans, or just that vague, uneasy feeling you can’t quite put your finger on. Suddenly, your mind’s off to the races—replaying conversations, imagining worst-case scenarios, and spinning stories out of thin air.
When that happens, it’s incredibly helpful to have what I like to call a “mental reset button.” Something simple you can rely on to pause, step back, and get some perspective.
Here are a few gentle, practical ways to interrupt overthinking in its tracks:
First, there’s the 5-5-5 Pause. Next time you catch your thoughts spiraling, stop and ask yourself: Will this matter in five minutes? Five days? Or five years? That quick check can really put worries in their place—and most of the time, you’ll see how temporary those concerns actually are.
Another tool is to simply name the thought. Silently say to yourself, “I’m worrying about tomorrow’s meeting,” or whatever’s swirling in your head. Just naming it helps create a bit of distance—almost like you’re stepping outside the thought, instead of getting tangled up in it.
And then there’s physical grounding. This one’s all about using your senses to pull you back into the present. Try noticing five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. It’s a quick way to interrupt those mental loops and bring your attention back to the here and now.
Picture this: someone’s lying awake, replaying a tough conversation from earlier. If they use the 5-5-5 Pause, they might realize that, honestly, the conversation’s going to fade away pretty quickly. Or, by naming the thought—“I’m ruminating about what I said”—they can gently nudge their focus back to something soothing, like the softness of their sheets or the steady sound of their own breath.
The point of these tools isn’t to force yourself to stop thinking altogether, or to slap on a layer of fake positivity. Instead, they offer a kind, practical way to acknowledge what’s happening—and then choose a different response.
With practice, these little interventions start to feel natural. And when they do, it becomes so much easier to find your way back to calm and clarity—even when life throws you a curveball.
